source_text: Superest, ne antiquitas suum quoque habuerit sacramentum, novitatem christianam recensere, quasi et de Deo aliam, ac proinde disciplina quoque aemulam, cujus sophia filios suos jugulare non norit. Plane alia in Christo et divinitas et voluntas et schola, martyria aut nulla in totum, aut aliter intelligenda mandarit, qui neminem ad hujusmodi discrimen hortetur, qui pro eo passis nihil repromittat, quia pati eos nolit. Et ideo praeceptorum principia deducens: Beati, inquit, qui persecutionem patiuntur ob justitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Hoc quidem absolute ad omnes, dehinc proprie ad Apostolos ipsos: Beati eritis cum vos dedecoraverint, et persecuti fuerint, et dixerint adversus vos omnia mala propter me; gaudete et exultate, quoniam merces vestra plurima in coelo: sic enim faciebant et prophetis patres eorum. Ut etiam prophetaret quod et ipsi occidi haberent ad exemplum prophetarum. Quanquam et si omnem hanc persecutionem conditionalem in solos tunc Apostolos destinasset, utique per illos cum toto sacramento, cum propagine nominis, cum traduce Spiritus Sancti in nos quoque spectasset etiam persecutionis obeundae disciplina, ut in haereditarios discipulos, et apostolici seminis frutices. Nam et rursus ad Apostolos dirigit: Ecce ego mitto vos tanquam oves in medio luporum; et: Cavete ab hominibus; tradent enim vos in consessus, et in synagogis suis flagellabunt vos, et ad praesides et reges perducemini, mei caussa, in testimonium illis et nationibus, etc. Cum autem subjicit: Tradet autem frater fratrem, et pater filium in mortem, et insurgent filii in parentes, et mortificabunt eos; manifeste iniquitatem istam in caeteros pronuntiavit, quam in Apostolis non invenimus. Nemo enim eorum aut fratrem aut patrem passus est traditorem, quod plerique jam nostri.
pass_a_gloss: It remains, that antiquity also had its own sacrament, to recount the newness of Christianity, as if there is also another God, and therefore a rival discipline, whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. Clearly, in Christ there is another divinity and will and school, either no martyrdoms at all, or they are to be understood in a different way, by the one who urges no one to this kind of danger, who promises nothing to those who suffer for him, because he does not want them to suffer. And therefore, drawing out the principles of teachings: Blessed, he says, are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, because the kingdom of heaven is theirs. This indeed absolutely to all, then properly to the Apostles themselves: Blessed will you be when they insult you, and persecute you, and speak all evil against you on account of me; rejoice and exult, because your reward is very great in heaven: for thus they did to the prophets, their fathers. So that he might also prophesy that they themselves would have to be killed, as an example of the prophets. Although even if he had destined this entire conditional persecution only to the Apostles at that time, certainly through them, with the whole sacrament, with the propagation of the name, with the tradition of the Holy Spirit to us, he would also have looked to the discipline of undergoing persecution, as to the heirs of disciples, and the fruits of apostolic seed. For again he directs to the Apostles: Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves; and: Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils, and they will flog you in their synagogues, and you will be led before governors and kings, for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations, etc. When, however, he adds: A brother will hand over a brother, and a father a son to death, and sons will rise up against parents, and will kill them; he clearly pronounced this wickedness against others, which we do not find in the Apostles. For none of them suffered a brother or father as a betrayer, which many of ours have already done.

pass_b_english: It remains to recount the newness of Christianity, because antiquity also had its own sacrament, as if there were another God and therefore a rival discipline whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. Clearly in Christ there is another divinity, another will, another school, which has commanded either no martyrdoms at all or martyrdoms understood differently, since it urges no one into such danger, promises nothing to those who suffer for it, because it does not want them to suffer. And so, drawing out the principles of his teachings, he says: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:10-12). This statement applies absolutely to everyone; then specifically to the Apostles themselves: Blessed will you be when they insult you, persecute you, and speak every kind of evil against you on my account; rejoice and be glad, because your reward is very great in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were your fathers (Matthew 5:11-12). This was so that he might also prophesy that they themselves would have to be killed, following the example of the prophets. Although even if he had destined this entire conditional persecution only for the Apostles at that time, he would certainly have looked through them—along with the whole sacrament, the propagation of the name, and the tradition of the Holy Spirit to us—to the discipline of undergoing persecution as well, treating us as heirs of the disciples and fruits of apostolic seed. For again he directs his words to the Apostles: Look, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; and: Beware of men, for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues, and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations (Matthew 10:16-18). But when he adds: A brother will hand over a brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death, he clearly pronounced this wickedness against others, a wickedness we do not find among the Apostles. For none of them suffered a brother or a father as a betrayer, which many of ours have already suffered.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (Matthew 5:10-12, 5:11-12, 10:16-18) which correspond to the quoted/alluded content in the Latin. All clauses, including the conditional argument regarding the Holy Spirit and the distinction between the Apostles and 'ours' (the current generation), are preserved.
